title: COP17: Tracking progress towards the UN’s 2030 nature targets
gist: Carbon Brief summarises a key UN report finding nations are falling short on 22 of 23 Kunming-Montreal nature targets ahead of the COP17 review in Armenia (19-30 October), with finance, harmful-subsidy and gender targets scoring lowest and ecosystem, wild-species and climate targets scoring highest. Data coverage is thin on many targets.

insights.claim: A key UN report finds the ambition to halt and reverse biodiversity loss will not be achieved by 2030 unless action 'accelerates rapidly', with nations falling short on 22 of 23 nature targets.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline narrative for COP17: expect pressure for stronger commitments, finance and enforcement.

insights.claim: COP17 in Armenia (19-30 October) will carry out the first global review of progress on the 23 targets, informed by the UN report and other findings.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Dated catalyst for nature-policy news flow.

insights.claim: Carbon Brief ranks national-level progress using figures from the report's second draft that were left out of the final version, scoring each target from 0 to 1 on self-reported data and key indicators.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: The score is a derived, self-reported-data metric, so treat it as a relative ranking rather than a verified measure.
insights.quote: left out of the final version

themes.theme: Finance and subsidy targets lag most

insights.claim: Target 19 (mobilise $200bn per year for biodiversity) scores 0.13 with only 25% of the way achieved per key indicators; the $20bn-by-2025 international milestone was 'likely not achieved', domestic spending as a share of GDP has declined, and private biodiversity finance has fallen since peaking in 2021.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Both public and private nature finance are heading the wrong way, supporting expectations of a contentious finance negotiation.

insights.claim: Target 18 (reduce harmful incentives by at least $500bn per year) scores 0.17; evidence suggests the 2025 milestone to identify harmful incentives 'was not achieved', with 'substantial' remaining value of harmful incentives and only 26% of relevant national targets on track.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Subsidy reform in agriculture, fishing and extractives remains largely unaddressed, so policy risk for those sectors is deferred, not removed.

insights.claim: Positive biodiversity incentives are growing in number even as scaling up remains limited, and finance is 'increasing' in both international and domestic terms despite being below required levels.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Small but rising green-incentive and funding flows are where early market opportunities appear.

insights.claim: Target 23 (gender equality) scores 0.13 and Target 17 (biosafety and biotechnology) scores 0.25, with implementation described as 'early stage' on gender and only 8% of countries reporting quantitative data on biosafety indicators.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: These cross-cutting targets are under-measured, so progress claims about them are weakly evidenced.

insights.claim: Target 14 (integrate biodiversity in political and sectoral decisions) scores 0.25 with a 'persistent disconnect between formal biodiversity policies and their effective implementation' and only 12% of countries reporting quantitative indicators.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Policy on paper not translating into practice suggests regulatory announcements overstate real change.
insights.quote: Persistent disconnect between formal biodiversity policies and their effective implementation.

insights.claim: Target 22 (include Indigenous peoples and local communities in decision-making) scores 0.25; monitoring is 'underdeveloped' and few countries include protection of environmental human rights defenders in national targets.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Rights and consent gaps are a project-level social-licence risk for land-use and extraction investments.

insights.claim: Target 15 (businesses monitor biodiversity impacts) scores 0.25: two-thirds of related national targets show 'no or insufficient progress' and mandatory reporting frameworks are lacking, though thousands of companies now disclose biodiversity-related risks and the number rises each year.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Voluntary nature-risk disclosure is growing but mandatory regimes are not in place; watch disclosure standards for large and transnational companies and financial institutions.

insights.claim: Target 16 (sustainable consumption) scores 0.38; measures on food waste, overconsumption and waste management are still under development, with weak producer responsibility and a lack of waste facilities, finance and enforcement.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Waste and producer-responsibility regulation is still being built, so compliance costs lie ahead.

themes.theme: Higher-scoring land, species and climate targets

insights.claim: Target 8 (minimise climate impacts on biodiversity) has the highest score at 0.75 and Target 5 (sustainable use and trade of wild species) scores 0.67, though only 18% of countries reported quantitative data on Target 8 and 33% on Target 5.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: The best-performing targets are also thinly measured, so high scores are partly an artefact of sparse data.
insights.locator: 8. Minimise impacts of climate change; 5. Ensure sustainable use

insights.claim: Targets 2 (restore 30% of degraded ecosystems) and 3 (conserve 30% of land and sea) score 0.5 and 0.38; protected-area expansion, especially marine and coastal, is good progress, but restoration is below needed levels and weaker in marine, coastal and freshwater areas than on land.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Spatial conservation targets are the most tractable, but restoration finance and monitoring are the bottleneck.

insights.claim: Target 4 (halt human-induced species extinction) shows 0% of the way towards the global target per key indicators, despite 70% of countries addressing at least half of its elements, so national intent is not translating into outcomes.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Plans-versus-outcomes divergence is starkest on extinction, a warning against reading policy coverage as progress.

insights.claim: Target 6 (halve introduction of invasive species) has most countries 'not on track to achieve national targets', with progress 'difficult to assess' and effective actions such as biosecurity measures 'not broadly in place'.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Invasive-species control, relevant to agriculture, trade and shipping, is weakly measured and poorly implemented.
insights.quote: not on track to achieve national targets
insights.locator: 6. Halve rate of introduction of invasive species

insights.claim: Target 10 (sustainable agriculture, aquaculture, fisheries and forestry) scores 0.5 but progress is 'not on track' for more than half of relevant national targets, with harmful subsidies, weak enforcement and climate pressures cited as barriers, and no assessment possible on sustainable aquaculture.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Primary-production sectors face continued shifts to biodiversity-friendly practice, but subsidies and enforcement shape the pace.
insights.quote: No assessment can be made on sustainable aquaculture.

insights.claim: Target 13 (equitable benefit-sharing from genetic resources, including digital sequence information) scores 0.38; legislative, policy and administrative requirements for access and benefit-sharing frameworks are in 'early stages', and regulatory challenges are among the most frequently cited obstacles.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Immature frameworks for genetic-data benefit-sharing are consistent with weak corporate payment flows.
insights.quote: Regulatory challenges are among the most frequently cited obstacles to implementation

insights.claim: Quantitative data reporting is thin on many targets (for example 8% of countries on biosafety, 12% on policy integration, 13% on gender, 15% on Indigenous participation), limiting any firm assessment of progress at the review.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Evidence gaps mean headline progress verdicts are uncertain; watch whether COP17 prioritises monitoring capacity.

insights.claim: Target 1 (plan and manage areas for biodiversity) scores 0.25, with 'major gaps' in integrating biodiversity into broader planning and expanding implementation beyond protected areas, even though 47% of countries have addressed at least half of its elements.
insights.speaker: Orla Dwyer, Tom Pearson
insights.so_what: Land-use planning integration is a gap that bears on development, infrastructure and real-estate siting.
insights.locator: 1. Plan and manage areas for biodiversity
